skill.name: pinchbench
skill.description: Run PinchBench to benchmark OpenClaw agents across real tasks, grade results, and optionally submit scores to the PinchBench leaderboard.
skill.summary: Benchmark OpenClaw agents with task suites, grading, and leaderboard upload.
skill.author: pinchbench

security_audit.summary: PinchBench is a legitimate benchmark runner, but it is not low risk. Confirmed issues include pipe-to-shell dependency installation, unsandboxed task grading code, external agent execution, token handling, and host metadata upload. Many documentation and task-rubric alerts are false positives, while binary assets remain manual-review blind spots.

remediation.issue: Docker build pipes a remote installer directly into a shell.
remediation.suggestion: Install uv from a pinned package or verify the downloaded installer with a published checksum before execution.

remediation.issue: Automated grading executes Python extracted from task markdown.
remediation.suggestion: Replace exec with structured checks or run grading code in a locked-down sandbox with no network and minimal filesystem access.

remediation.issue: Leaderboard upload sends system metadata and uses credential headers.
remediation.suggestion: Make upload opt-in, document every submitted field, minimize metadata, and warn when PINCHBENCH_SERVER_URL is overridden.

remediation.issue: Registration tokens are stored under the skill directory.
remediation.suggestion: Store tokens in an OS credential store or user config directory with restrictive permissions.

remediation.issue: Workspace setup copies installed skills and deletes benchmark state.
remediation.suggestion: Use a dedicated sandbox, allowlist copied fixtures, and refuse non-benchmark agent IDs before deletion.

remediation.issue: Binary assets could not be reviewed by static text analysis.
remediation.suggestion: Manually review the PNG, PDF, and XLSX assets and publish trusted hashes for release artifacts.

semantic_findings.title: System Metadata Uploaded With Results
semantic_findings.description: When uploads are enabled, the payload includes metadata.system and records OS, CPU, Python, memory, and a hostname hash. This goes beyond benchmark scores and may identify the host environment.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The upload payload explicitly includes collect_system_metadata output. The metadata function records platform, CPU, memory, Python, and hostname-derived data.

semantic_findings.title: Registration Token Stored In Skill Directory
semantic_findings.description: The registration helper writes the returned token to scripts/.pinchbench/config.json under the skill directory. Tokens in an installed skill tree can be accidentally shared or read by benchmarked agents.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The config path is inside the scripts directory and save_token_config writes the token there. _resolve_token later reads that stored token for uploads.

semantic_findings.title: Installed Skills Copied Into Benchmark Workspace
semantic_findings.description: prepare_task_workspace copies every directory under ~/.openclaw/workspace/skills into the benchmark workspace. This may expose private skill content or embedded credentials to the benchmarked model during tasks.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The code iterates over the user skill directory and copies each skill directory into the agent workspace. No allowlist or secret filtering is visible in that block.

semantic_findings.title: Agent Session Transcripts Deleted Without Confirmation
semantic_findings.description: cleanup_agent_sessions removes stored session transcript files and sessions.json for the target agent. If the target agent ID collides with a real agent, benchmark runs can delete local conversation history.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The deletion code is explicit and is called before benchmark and judge runs. The risk is reduced because agent IDs are normally benchmark-prefixed, but collision is still possible.

content.value_statement: Agent teams need repeatable evidence before comparing models. PinchBench runs real-world OpenClaw tasks, grades outcomes, and can publish results to a leaderboard.
actual_capabilities: Runs 23 bundled benchmark tasks across productivity, research, writing, coding, email, and file workflows.
Creates or reuses OpenClaw agents for selected model identifiers.
Grades tasks with automated checks, LLM judge rubrics, or hybrid scoring.
Records task transcripts, timing, token use, cost, and score summaries.
Saves local result files and can upload authorized submissions to PinchBench.
limitations: Requires Python, uv, and a working OpenClaw installation.
Some tasks call external services or model APIs, which can add cost.
Leaderboard upload requires a PinchBench token and sends run metadata.
Automated grading executes bundled task check code, so review tasks before running.

use_cases.title: Compare Agent Models
use_cases.description: Run the same task suite across models and compare score, cost, time, and category performance.

use_cases.title: Validate OpenClaw Setup
use_cases.description: Check that an OpenClaw installation can handle tools, memory, files, research, and multi-step workflows.

use_cases.title: Publish Benchmark Results
use_cases.description: Generate reproducible local results and submit authorized runs to the PinchBench leaderboard.

prompt_templates.title: Run A Quick Benchmark
prompt_templates.prompt: Use PinchBench to run the automated-only suite for [model id] with uploads disabled. Summarize the final score and failed tasks.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Two Models
prompt_templates.prompt: Run PinchBench for [model A] and [model B] using the same suite and run count. Compare category scores, cost, and time.

prompt_templates.title: Upload A Previous Run
prompt_templates.prompt: Validate my saved PinchBench result at [file path], upload it to the leaderboard, and report the submission link.

prompt_templates.title: Audit A Custom Task
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my new PinchBench task file for clear grading, safe workspace files, and reproducible behavior before I run it.

output_examples.input: Run the automated-only suite for openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4 without uploading results.
output_examples.output: PinchBench completed the automated suite. The report showed the overall score, failed tasks, timing, and upload was skipped.

output_examples.input: Compare two model runs using the same task suite.
output: Model A had stronger file and coding task scores.
Model B used fewer tokens and finished faster.
The summary highlighted score, cost, and timeout differences.

output_examples.input: Upload a saved benchmark result after registration.
output_examples.output: The saved run was submitted to PinchBench and the response included submission status, rank, and leaderboard link.

best_practices: Start with automated-only and uploads disabled when testing a new model.
Use the same suite, run count, and timeout multiplier when comparing models.
Review task files and upload settings before running community benchmarks.
anti_patterns: Running all tasks with uploads enabled before validating local behavior.
Comparing models with different task suites or timeout settings.
Sharing result files without checking transcripts and system metadata.

faq.question: What does PinchBench evaluate?
faq.answer: It evaluates how OpenClaw agents complete real tasks across files, research, writing, coding, email, memory, and workflows.

faq.question: Does it require OpenClaw?
faq.answer: Yes. The runner creates or reuses OpenClaw agents and sends benchmark prompts through the OpenClaw command line tool.

faq.question: Can I run it without uploading results?
faq.answer: Yes. Use the no-upload option when you want local result files only.

faq.question: How are tasks graded?
faq.answer: Tasks use automated Python checks, LLM judge rubrics, or a hybrid of both methods.

faq.question: What data may leave my machine?
faq.answer: Uploads can include scores, timing, usage, task metadata, system metadata, and authentication headers for PinchBench.

faq.question: Should I run it in a production workspace?
faq.answer: No. Use a dedicated sandbox because it creates workspaces, deletes benchmark state, and executes grading code.
